name: Fatima Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Fatima, 58, an experienced mid-level developer at a tech company that builds elevator-alert software. I have a bachelor's degree and a good wage, and I use AI every day to draft tests before checking the technician's signed inspection record. A sensor change once looked like a motor fault, so I do not trust a green screen on its own. My partner is a physical therapist, our children are grown, and the home is paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the lift technicians that an alarm means something only when it matches their inspection record. I maintain a tech company's elevator-alert software and use AI every day to sketch tests, but I check a motor fault against the technician's signed log.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI stays a modest aid, I expect to keep my experienced mid-level post. My pay is high, my partner works full-time as a physical therapist, our home is paid for, and we have nine months of expenses saved; there are many similar firms nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep resolving false motor alarms against field inspection logs. We would save another 150 monthly while both wages hold, as I do not yet have verified retirement figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about this version. A harmless-looking false clear can still leave somebody stuck between floors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why did you keep the alarm open?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One lift sent a motor-overheat alert just after a technician replaced the sensor. The signed log showed the sensor change, and I kept the lift's motor alarm open until the technician checked the motor itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children fund retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children have their own places and bills. We trade family dinners, not monthly transfers for our retirement.

I'd keep **false clears** visible when a sensor has just changed.
think: I expect **two wages** and my mid-level role to hold under mild AI change.
I have **nine months saved** and many nearby software firms.
do: Keep **resolving false alarms** against technicians' signed inspection logs.
Save **150 extra monthly** while both wages hold; check retirement statements before deciding when to stop.
feel: **Calm** about present work, attentive to stranded passengers.

fieldNote: **Nine months saved** and high pay support calm alongside a second steady wage and paid-off home.

steps.text: Keep checking motor alarms against signed technician inspection logs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI could write alert rules and answer building managers quickly, but someone has to check a false clear against a real inspection. I would try it on known faults before a live lift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My experienced role may change, and the company could ask fewer developers to watch routine alarms. Nine months saved gives room to learn, but losing my larger wage would still change our retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the service manager to approve a six-week comparison of AI alerts with old signed technician logs, including the changed-sensor case and a real stalled lift. If it catches both without hiding a safety fault, I'd use it on one building with a named technician able to halt release; we'd delay a planned conservatory until staffing and paid hours are clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my job, but I can test a tool instead of guessing. A lift should not be a beta test for a building manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which two cases must stay separate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The stalled lift case had a real motor heat rise, not a sensor swap. Both cases must stay separate or the new rule will turn one into a false clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What spending can wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The conservatory is optional and no builder is booked. My partner and I would keep the cash liquid until we know whether both wages continue.

I'd require **technician stop authority** on any new rule.

fieldNote: **Routine alarm code** faces AI, so her own paid hours could shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI by 2028 could write lift-alert code before maintenance robots arrive around 2031. Building managers still need a real person to explain a faulty alarm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my mid-level post could be cut quickly if the system writes and tests ordinary alerts. My partner's therapy wage covers the basics, and nine months saved gives search time, but neither is a verified pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask four nearby software firms and the lift service company about actual paid fault-review or safety-test vacancies and written wages. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd take only a signed job whose pay with my partner's covers utilities, food, health and travel; if none qualifies, I'd seek other available paid local work while using savings and check health-cover dates before a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing my wage earlier than planned. A lift motor still needs checking, but that does not mean a service company has a paid desk for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show another employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the anonymised sensor-swap case and why I kept the motor alarm open. It proves I checked the physical record rather than accepting a convenient green status.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What terms matter to your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner wants the new role's start date and health cover in writing. A good yearly salary with six unpaid weeks between jobs would not settle our bills.

I'd check **real paid vacancies** before naming another job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 gives me time to learn which firms still pay for lift-safety test records. Thinking AI reaches code then, and maintenance robots follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could shift to a safety-test job at another software firm, but I will not assume a vacancy or a wage matching mine. Our home is paid for, yet my partner and I still need a reliable income before retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the signed motor-fault case in an anonymised work sample, with employer permission before showing it outside. I'd ask three nearby firms for posted safety-test duties and pay; if one offers a signed role whose combined wages cover utilities, food, health and travel without a cover gap, I'd apply and take it after 2031, otherwise keep my paid development post while offered and seek other paid local work if cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with time to ask for real terms. I would not leave a wage for a job title that only exists in a recruitment slide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What can appear in the work sample?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The sample would include the sensor replacement, the still-open alarm and the technician's later motor check, with names and building address removed. I need the firm's permission before carrying even an anonymised incident out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner compare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would compare the start date and insurance details with the therapy rota. We can manage a short search, but not pretend a pay gap has no cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 might bring me to 68, but thinking AI will reach lift-alert code before robots do physical maintenance around 2039. A signed inspection remains useful even if I am not writing the rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Today our two wages, paid-off home and nine-month reserve feel secure. I have not verified our pension amounts, and I cannot assume the firm will keep my salary for another decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the motor-fault test and save 150 monthly while both wages hold, then request both retirement statements and compare verified income with utilities, food, health and travel. In the first year after 2036 I'd stop paid work only if those figures cover bills; otherwise I'd keep an offered paid role or seek actual nearby vacancies without counting our children's income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about distant employment, though current bills are covered. I would rather leave a clear alarm trail than a stack of confident machine explanations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the test record say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The test record should say sensor changed, alarm remained open and technician checked the motor. A new developer can see why those are three separate events.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children contribute?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children can visit and ask about my work, but their pay belongs to their homes. We will not turn a family dinner into a retirement bill.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the company could cut alert-code posts before another firm offers paid safety work. Written notice, actual vacancies and continuous health cover would help us use savings without guessing about retirement.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who signs the lift safe after software changes. A technician's inspection is a real event; a green dashboard is only a report of one.

headlineQuote: A technician's inspection is a real event; a green dashboard is only a report of one.
portrait: Fatima, **58**, is an experienced mid-level lift-alert developer with a bachelor's degree who checks AI test drafts against signed inspections.
Her **higher wage**, partner's therapy pay, paid-off home, nine-month reserve and many nearby firms secure present bills.
She uses AI **daily** but requires service-manager approval, two fault tests and technician stop power before one-building deployment.
Fast 2028 AGI **alarms** her; a new safety-test role needs employer-cleared evidence, a posted vacancy, signed wages and health cover.
She will **verify retirement income** before stopping work and does not budget her grown children's pay.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her alert-code wage before another firm offers paid safety work.
whatWouldHelp: **Written cut notice**, real paid vacancies and continuous health cover would help her plan.
